result.markdown: --- title: "Session 4 — Nonresponse, Raking and Replicate Weights" subtitle: "Nonresponse adjustment · weight diagnostics · post-stratification and raking · trimming · replicate weights · Lab 4" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: weight = 1 / selection probability - Today: how the **final weights** are built, and how to **check** them - By the end you can: - measure **nonresponse** and adjust for it - compute **weight diagnostics** - **rake** weights to known population totals - use **replicate weights** for variances ::: # Topic 1 — Nonresponse {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Who responds? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} adults |> group_by(sex) |> summarise(n = n(), response_rate = round(mean(responded), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 3 sex n response_rate 1 Female 1251 0.79 2 Male 1253 0.69 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} adults |> group_by(age_grp) |> summarise(n = n(), response_rate = round(mean(responded), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 age_grp n response_rate 1 18-29 476 0.64 2 30-44 840 0.75 3 45-59 844 0.75 4 60+ 344 0.82 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Overall response is **74%**, but **men 69%** vs **women 79%**, and young adults least. If you ignore this, **men and the young are under-represented**: any outcome that differs by sex or age is **biased**. ::: ## The adjustment ::: {.eq} final weight = design weight / response rate in the weighting cell ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cells <- adults |> group_by(age_grp, sex, residence) |> summarise(rr = mean(responded), .groups = "drop") adj <- adults |> filter(responded == 1) |> left_join(cells, by = c("age_grp", "sex", "residence")) |> mutate(w_new = design_weight / rr) all.equal(adj$w_new, adj$weight, tolerance = 0.001) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Cells use variables **known for everyone sampled** (age, sex, residence) - Each respondent also **stands for the nonrespondents in the same cell** - It cannot fix nonresponse that depends on things you did **not** measure (e.g. education here) ::: # Topic 2 — Diagnostics and raking {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Check the weights ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} w <- weights(des) c(min = min(w), median = median(w), max = max(w), cv = sd(w) / mean(w), n_eff_kish = sum(w)^2 / sum(w^2)) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` min median max cv n_eff_kish 93.44 241.30 483.93 0.43 1563.23 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} CV **0.43**; the **Kish effective sample size** is about **1,560** of 1,853: unequal weights cost about **16% of the precision**. Very large weights (or CV above about 1) are a warning: look at **who** has them. ::: ## Raking (calibration) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pop_age <- pop |> filter(variable == "age_group") |> transmute(age_grp = level, Freq = adults) pop_sex <- pop |> filter(variable == "sex") |> transmute(sex = level, Freq = adults) pop_edu <- pop |> filter(variable == "education") |> transmute(education = level, Freq = adults) des_r <- rake(des, list(~age_grp, ~sex, ~education), list(pop_age, pop_sex, pop_edu)) round(rbind(before = prop.table(svytable(~education, des)), after = prop.table(svytable(~education, des_r)), census = setNames(pop_edu$Freq / sum(pop_edu$Freq), pop_edu$education)[levels(resp$education)]), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None Primary Secondary+ before 0.286 0.364 0.35 after 0.272 0.369 0.36 census 0.272 0.369 0.36 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Raking** adjusts the weights step by step until the weighted **margins** equal **known population totals** (a census) - Use when the **joint** distribution is unknown but the **margins** are known - Here the change in the prevalence is small (**19.95% to 19.74%**): raking matters most when nonresponse is related to the outcome - Check afterwards that the weights are **not too variable** ::: ## Trimming ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} des_t <- trimWeights(des_r, upper = 1.5 * median(weights(des_r)), strict = TRUE) c(before = max(weights(des_r)), after = max(weights(des_t))) |> round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` before after 484 344 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} **Trimming** caps very large weights: it trades a little **bias** for less **variance**. Report it if you do it. ::: # Topic 3 — Replicate weights {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Another way to get the variance ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) rep_des <- as.svrepdesign(des, type = "bootstrap", replicates = 200) c(taylor = SE(svymean(~hypertension, des)), bootstrap = SE(svymean(~hypertension, rep_des))) |> round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` taylor bootstrap 0.0149 0.0153 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - The estimate is recomputed on **many re-weighted sub-samples** (jackknife, BRR, bootstrap); the spread gives the SE - Many data providers release **replicate weights** instead of strata and PSUs (to protect identity): then use `svrepdesign()` - Works for **complex statistics** (medians, ratios, differences) where formulas are hard - Same answer as Taylor linearisation here (**0.0149** vs **0.015**) ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 4 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `survey-workshop/labs/lab4_weights.R` - response by sex and age; rebuild the adjusted weight - effective sample size, raking, trimming - bootstrap replicate weights ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v4q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="kyw2r2.dxglfb" data-show="TWVuIGFyZSB1bmRlci1yZXByZXNlbnRlZCwgYW5kIHJlc3VsdHMgdGhhdCBkaWZmZXIgYnkg c2V4IGFyZSBiaWFzZWQ=" data-explain="Tm9ucmVzcG9uc2UgdGhhdCBkZXBlbmRzIG9uIHNleCBhbmQgb24gdGhlIG91dGNvbWUgZGlz dG9ydHMgdGhlIHNhbXBsZS4gV2VpZ2h0cyBhZGp1c3RlZCBmb3Igbm9ucmVzcG9uc2UgZ2l2 ZSByZXNwb25kZW50cyB0aGUgd2VpZ2h0IG9mIHRoZSBtaXNzaW5nIG9uZXMu"} Men respond less often than women. If this is ignored, what is likely to happen? - Men are over-represented, and results that differ by sex are unbiased - The sample size falls, but the estimates stay unbiased - Men are under-represented, and results that differ by sex are biased - The standard errors become zero for all the estimates ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v4q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="kywfzq.dxgzwn" data-show="RWFjaCByZXNwb25kZW50IGFsc28gc3RhbmRzIGZvciB0aGUgbm9ucmVzcG9uZGVudHMgaW4g dGhlIGNlbGw=" data-explain="QSBjZWxsIHdpdGggYSA1MCUgcmVzcG9uc2UgcmF0ZSBoYXMgaGFsZiBvZiBpdHMgc2FtcGxl IG1pc3NpbmcsIHNvIGVhY2ggcmVzcG9uZGVudCB3ZWlnaHMgdHdpY2UgYXMgbXVjaDogdGhl IHdlaWdodHMga2VlcCBhZGRpbmcgdXAgdG8gdGhlIGNlbGwgdG90YWwu"} In the nonresponse adjustment, why is the design weight divided by the cell response rate? - The weights then add up to the number of respondents who answered - Each respondent also stands for the nonrespondents in the cell - Cells with high response rates need smaller standard errors in the analysis - It converts the weights into selection probabilities for the PSUs in the cell ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v4q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="kywt8g.dxhee1" data-show="SXQgYWRqdXN0cyB0aGUgd2VpZ2h0cyB1bnRpbCB0aGUgd2VpZ2h0ZWQgbWFyZ2lucyBtYXRj aCBrbm93biB0b3RhbHM=" data-explain="UmFraW5nLCBvciBpdGVyYXRpdmUgcHJvcG9ydGlvbmFsIGZpdHRpbmcsIHJlc2NhbGVzIHRo ZSB3ZWlnaHRzIHN0ZXAgYnkgc3RlcCB0byByZXByb2R1Y2Uga25vd24gbWFyZ2lucyBzdWNo IGFzIHRoZSBjZW5zdXMgYWdlLCBzZXggYW5kIGVkdWNhdGlvbiBkaXN0cmlidXRpb24u"} What does raking (calibration) do? - It drops respondents at random until the sample margins match the population - It replaces missing answers by values predicted from the population totals - It adjusts the weights until the weighted margins match known totals - It divides the weights by their mean so that they add up to one ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v4q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="kyx6h6.dxhsvf" data-show="VW5lcXVhbCB3ZWlnaHRzIGNvc3QgYWJvdXQgMTYlIG9mIHRoZSBwcmVjaXNpb24gb2YgdGhl IHNhbXBsZQ==" data-explain="VGhlIEtpc2ggZm9ybXVsYSBtZWFzdXJlcyB0aGUgbG9zcyBvZiBwcmVjaXNpb24gZnJvbSB2 YXJpYWJsZSB3ZWlnaHRzIGFsb25lLiBDbHVzdGVyaW5nIGNvbWVzIG9uIHRvcCBvZiB0aGlz IGFuZCBpcyBwYXJ0IG9mIHRoZSBkZXNpZ24gZWZmZWN0Lg=="} The Kish effective sample size is 1,563 for 1,853 respondents. How is this best read? - The survey lost 16% of its respondents because of nonresponse - The design effect due to clustering is 1.16 - The weights should be divided by 1.16 before analysis - Unequal weights cost about 16% of the precision of the sample ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v4q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="kyxjps.dxi7cp" data-show="VG8gZ2V0IHZhcmlhbmNlcyBieSByZWNhbGN1bGF0aW5nIHRoZSBlc3RpbWF0ZSBvbiByZS13 ZWlnaHRlZCBzdWItc2FtcGxlcw==" data-explain="VGhlIGVzdGltYXRlIGlzIHJlY29tcHV0ZWQgd2l0aCBlYWNoIHNldCBvZiByZXBsaWNhdGUg d2VpZ2h0cywgYW5kIHRoZSB2YXJpYXRpb24gYmV0d2VlbiB0aGUgcmVwbGljYXRlcyBnaXZl cyB0aGUgc3RhbmRhcmQgZXJyb3IuIFRoZXkgZG8gbm90IGNoYW5nZSB0aGUgcG9pbnQgZXN0 aW1hdGUu"} What are replicate weights used for? - To get variances by recalculating the estimate on re-weighted sub-samples - To replace the usual weights with equal weights for all of the respondents - To fill in the answers of adults who did not respond to the survey in the field - To remove the bias that the usual weights leave in the point estimate ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Nonresponse adjustment**: design weight / cell response rate - **Check the weights**: range, CV, Kish n~eff~ - **Raking** to known margins; **trimming** extreme weights - **Replicate weights** (`as.svrepdesign`, `svrepdesign`) give variances without strata and PSU - Weights cannot fix nonresponse on **unmeasured** variables ::: **Next:** Session 5: choosing, checking and reporting

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
